title: Characterization of an IncF2:A-:B- plasmid harboring fosA3 gene in a Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli O26:H11 isolated from a child with diarrhea in Japan
content:
Abstract
The efficacy of antimicrobial therapy against Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) infections has been a matter of global debate. In Japan, fosfomycin is often prescribed for pediatric patients to prevent life-threatening sequelae. Recently, E. coli strains harboring plasmid-mediated fosfomycin-resistant genes (fos genes) have been disseminated worldwide, yet the prevalence of these genes among STEC remains unclear. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of fosfomycin resistance among STEC strains isolated from humans, as well as to analyze the molecular characteristics of a conjugative plasmid carrying a fos gene in a STEC strain. Two fosfomycin-resistant STEC O26:H11 strains were identified among 206 STECs by the disk diffusion method. The primary fos gene, fosA3, was identified on an IncF2:A-:B- plasmid in one strain. This plasmid could be transferred to recipients, and the frequency of transfer was higher for STEC O26 recipients compared to STEC O157 recipients. Sequence-based comparative analysis of the plasmid suggested horizontal transfer of fosA3 gene among diverse bacterial strains, with insertion sequences playing a pivotal role in its mobilization. These findings suggest the possibility of fosA3 gene disseminating among diverse STEC strains and emphasize the importance of monitoring fosfomycin resistance and characterizing resistance plasmids in STEC strains.

title: Comparison of nine agar media for the recovery of shigatoxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) from the food
content:
Abstract
Pathogenic Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) are a major public health concern and a key issue for the agri-food sector. However, their isolation remains challenging because STEC lack distinctive biochemical characteristics that clearly differentiate them from other Escherichia coli. This study evaluated the performance of nine commonly used agar media for STEC isolation using three types of samples: pure cultures, experimentally spiked food matrices, and naturally contaminated foods. Two isolation approaches were compared: direct streaking and immuno-separation followed by plating. In pure cultures, five media (TBX, SMAC, Rainbow®AgarO157, CHROMID®EHEC Agar, and IDEA™ STEC with or without cefixime-tellurite) achieved complete recovery, whereas CT-CHROMID®EHEC, CT-SMAC and CHROMagarTMSTEC agar inhibited the growth of several strains, particularly those sensitive to tellurite. In food matrices, immunomagnetic separation resulted in high and comparable detection rates across media (80–95%; n = 16/20–19/20). In contrast, direct streaking showed highly variable recovery depending on the medium (29–100%; n = 7/20–20/20). These results demonstrate that combining selective and non-selective media improves STEC detection. Immuno separation enhances recovery of key serogroups, while IDEA STEC enables additional differentiation through halo formation. The observed variability in toxin production suggests that environmental and physiological factors influence STEC detection.

title: Community-Acquired Infection Caused by mcr-1 and blaOXA-48-Producing Escherichia coli: A Case Highlighting Limitations of Selective Susceptibility Testing
content:
Abstract
Selective antimicrobial susceptibility supports antimicrobial stewardship strategy but may have limitations in high-resistance prevalence settings. We report a community-acquired infection of necrotic metastatic inguinal lymphadenopathy caused by two mcr-producing Escherichia coli isolates, including one blaOXA-48 producer. Initial selective susceptibility testing delayed recognition of clinically relevant resistance. This case highlights the risk of silent community dissemination of high-priority resistance determinants. It underscores the need for context-adapted susceptibility reporting to balance antimicrobial stewardship and resistance surveillance.

title: Eddy covariance diverges from inventory and model-based estimates of soil organic carbon stock change across five  crop rotations in Belgian cropland
content:
Eddy covariance diverges from inventory and model-based estimates of soil organic carbon stock change across five crop rotations in Belgian cropland
Quentin Beauclaire, Bernard Longdoz, Laura Delhez, Bruna Winck, Benjamin Loubet, Yue Zhou, Marmar Sabetizade, Neo Arquin, Nicolas Saby, and Bernard Heinesch
Biogeosciences, 23, 7345–7374, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7345-2026, 2026
We studied how soil organic carbon stocks changed over 21 years in a Belgian cropland by combining soil sampling, a soil carbon model, and measurements from a flux tower. The soil appeared mostly stable overall, but the flux-tower approach suggested much larger carbon losses than the other methods. Our results show that using several approaches together is important to better understand soil organic carbon changes and to identify farming practices that either build up or reduce soil carbon.

title: Impact of Typhoons Hato and Pakhar (2017) on Particulate Organic Carbon Transport in the Pearl River Estuary, China: A Numerical Study
content:
Abstract
Estuaries play a crucial role in the transport and cycling of particulate organic carbon (POC) from terrestrial ecosystems to the ocean. However, an understanding of the processes controlling POC dynamics under extreme weather conditions is still lacking. In this study, we established a high‐resolution, coupled atmosphere–ocean–biogeochemistry modeling system for the Pearl River Estuary to investigate the mechanisms controlling POC dynamics during a strong successive typhoon event (Hato and Pakhar, 2017). Our simulation results show that before the typhoons, the POC distribution was characterized by two distinct maxima, sustained by terrestrial inputs and marine production, respectively. However, during the typhoons, strong hydrodynamic conditions and reduced light availability suppressed local primary production, leading to an increase in the dominance of terrestrial POC. In Lingding Bay (LB) and the Western Four Outlets (WFO), POC was mainly supported by regenerated production, whereas in the shallow coastal region (SCR) outside the estuarine, new and regenerated production played an equal role. Regarding POC sinks, zooplankton excretion served as the dominant sink in the outer LB and SCR regions, while sediment denitrification played an equally significant role in the inner LB and WFO. Budget analysis revealed that although the estuary acted as a weak carbon source on an annual basis, successive typhoons can transform it into a weak carbon sink. Our simulation provides novel insights into the impact of extreme weather on POC within estuaries, benefiting the maintenance of ecological health and the development of effective water quality management strategies under global warming.

title: Interactions Between the Mesoscale Eddy Dipole and Eastward Jet in the Western South China Sea
content:
Abstract
The mesoscale eddy dipole (MED) in the western South China Sea is characterized by a seasonal pair of cold and warm eddies, which typically appear off the Vietnam coast from July to September, accompanied by an eastward jet (EJ) traversing the MED between 11°N and 12°N. However, detailed investigations into the interactions between the MED and EJ remain limited in previous studies. In this study, the interactions between the MED and EJ in 2011 are examined from both morphologic and energetic perspectives using the Oceanic Regional Circulation and Tidal Model. Variations in their intensity and position are strongly correlated. Multiscale energy transfer analysis reveals a notable positive energy cascade from the EJ to the MED. Mixed barotropic and baroclinic instabilities, primarily occurring in the upstream region of the EJ, promote the formation and development of the MED. In contrast, in the mid‐downstream region, part of kinetic energy is inversely transferred from mesoscale eddies to the large‐scale circulation, facilitating the stretching and intensification of the EJ. The distribution of eddy–mean flow energy transfer is distinctly anisotropic, with stronger energetic interactions in the upstream part of the EJ horizontally and within the cold eddy of the MED meridionally. This study advances our understanding and underscores the need for greater attention to this highly seasonal eddy–mean flow dynamic system.

title: Nitrate Transport Across the Northern Gulf of Mexico Shelf During Historically High Mississippi River Discharge
content:
Abstract
This study characterizes the spatial and seasonal dynamics of radium isotopes (223Ra, 224Ra, and 228Ra) and nitrate plus nitrite (NO3− + NO2−) transport on the northern Gulf of Mexico shelf during 2019, when the Mississippi River remained at flood stage for 226 days. Sampling focused on two contrasting shelf settings: the Atchafalaya‐influenced Wax Lake Delta region and the Mississippi‐influenced Barataria Basin (BB) region. High river discharge in June produced elevated radium activities and stronger low‐salinity nitrate enrichment relative to September. Radium activity ratios yielded apparent surface‐water ages of approximately 5–10 days during peak discharge, indicating rapid transport of river‐associated constituents across the shelf. We further compared radium‐derived apparent effective mixing estimates with ADCP‐based advective nitrate fluxes measured at a fixed shelf location. These two approaches emphasize different, but not fully separable, components of transport in a dynamic river plume system. The radium‐derived estimates are model‐dependent and may include effects of unresolved plume advection, whereas ADCP‐derived fluxes represent velocity‐driven transport of nitrate fields that have already been shaped by mixing and dispersion. A first‐order mass balance suggests that the shallow Louisiana shelf retained or transformed only 39% of riverine nitrate during the high‐discharge period, with the rest being transported rapidly to deeper water beyond 50 m isobath.

title: Synoptic Wind‐Dependent Sampling Asymmetry Biases Satellite Sea Surface Chlorophyll‐a in the Mid‐to‐High‐Latitude North Pacific and North Atlantic
content:
Abstract
Satellite observations of sea surface chlorophyll‐a concentration (SChl) provide a basin‐scale record for interpreting marine productivity and upper ocean biogeochemical variability. However, clouds and other observational limits create gaps in SChl retrieval, which can bias the SChl record, especially in cloud‐prone mid‐to‐high‐latitude oceans. Here, we use satellite SChl data from 2010 to 2019 to quantify sampling bias associated with synoptic‐scale wind speed conditions. In winter, compared with low wind speed conditions, high wind speed conditions are often cloudier, yielding fewer valid retrievals of SChl. At the same time, observed SChl is generally lower under high wind speed conditions across the mid‐to‐high latitudes of the North Atlantic and the North Pacific. Together, these differences bias mean SChl upward. The largest bias occurs in winter, when the bias of gyre‐mean SChl is about 1.4%, with local values exceeding 10%. The resulting SChl bias also propagates into satellite‐based estimates of ocean productivity.

title: The Cold Fresh Pulse in the Northwest Atlantic in 2023/2024
content:
Abstract
The Northwest Atlantic Ocean has been warming at an accelerated rate since 2010. However, in summer 2023 a cold fresh signal concentrated along the shelfbreak advected into the Middle Atlantic Bight from the Scotian Shelf and Grand Banks region. By spring of 2024 the entire continental shelf in the Middle Atlantic Bight had a significant fresh salinity anomaly. A second cold fresh pulse appeared primarily located over the continental slope in May 2024. Shipboard observations in early June 2024 show that near surface salinity across the entire slope region was typical of mid‐shelf salinities (31–33 PSU). The fresh anomalies were greatly reduced by October 2024. The unusual water mass conditions, including cold anomalies in May/June 2024, led to major changes to the shelf/slope ecosystem in 2024 including significant decreases in shortfin and longfin squid landings and the re‐appearance of cold water fish such as mackerel and herring. There were direct economic impacts in terms of reduced revenue to major fishing ports in the northeast U.S. In addition, a substantial fresh water anomaly was injected into the Gulf Stream, with potential impacts further downstream in terms of stratification in the North Atlantic.

title: When Hybrids Take an Intermediate Route: Genetic Ancestry Shapes Migration Across a Seabird Contact Zone
content:
ABSTRACT
Contact zones, where related taxa breed sympatrically, provide natural laboratories for studying phylogeography and speciation. In migratory species, these systems offer unique opportunities to disentangle the relative roles of genetic and social factors in migratory behaviour. Cory's (Calonectris borealis) and Scopoli's shearwaters (C. diomedea) are closely related long‐distance migrants that breed allopatrically across most of their ranges but occur sympatrically in the Alboran Sea. Here, we tested whether the migratory strategies of these shearwaters are determined primarily by their genetic ancestry or by the social environment of their breeding colony. We used light‐level geolocators to track the annual migration of 50 individuals (127 tracks) from six breeding colonies: four sympatric colonies within the Alboran contact zone and one allopatric colony of each species. We also generated whole‐genome sequencing data for 58 individuals (including all 50 tracked birds) to infer species ancestry and identify hybrids. Most Cory's shearwaters wintered in subtropical Atlantic upwelling systems along the African and South American coasts, whereas most Scopoli's shearwaters wintered in tropical waters off West Africa. The two taxa partially overlapped in the Sahelian upwelling and Angolan waters. Individuals breeding in the contact zone exhibited migration strategies that matched their genomic ancestry rather than the colony's predominant pattern. Most importantly, we identified seven recent hybrids between the two taxa, representing 17.5% of the sampled individuals in the contact zone. These hybrids exhibited intermediate migratory strategies, indicating a strong genetic determination of migratory behaviour. The overlap in wintering areas may increase opportunities for interspecific interactions before arrival at the breeding colonies, potentially promoting hybridisation. Our study demonstrates that migratory strategies are strongly influenced by genetic background in long‐distance migratory seabirds and suggests that weak migratory connectivity among populations facilitates hybridisation in contact zones.

title: Functional Diversity Responses to Temperature Vary Spatially and With Protection Status in Wintering Waterbird Assemblages
content:
Using > 45,000 waterbird censuses at 2792 European sites, we found functional diversity has increased over time and in warmer winters, but functional redundancy has declined. Ramsar and Special Protection Area sites had the greatest increase in functional richness but the greatest decline in functional redundancy in warmer winters, especially further north and east. This study suggests rising temperatures could alter the functional diversity and resilience of waterbird assemblages across Europe.

ABSTRACT
Wetlands support disproportionately high biodiversity, including waterbirds, which underpin key ecological functions and regulatory services. This has led to efforts to protect these crucial sites, but whether these protections can maintain waterbird assemblages in the face of new threats such as climate change is poorly understood. Here, we calculated functional redundancy and three metrics of functional diversity from over 45,000 waterbird censuses, spanning four decades of rising winter temperatures for 2792 protected and unprotected sites in Europe. We modelled the effect of average winter temperature and the trend over time for each of these metrics. Our results suggest functional diversity generally increased in warmer winters and over time, but redundancy declined, and the effect of temperature varied spatially and between levels of protection. This suggests abundance and distribution shifts due to climate change are altering functional diversity and resilience of waterbird assemblages both inside and outside protected areas across Europe.

title: Divergent Spatial and Temporal Sensitivities of Forest Biomass to Climate Challenge Space‐For‐Time Assumptions and Models
content:
Spatial and temporal climate–biomass relationships diverge globally: spatial gradients explain more variation and yield much stronger sensitivities than interannual temporal variability. This mismatch propagates into future projections, with spatial relationships indicating forest biomass losses while temporal extrapolations and Earth system models project little change or gains.

ABSTRACT
Understanding and projecting forest carbon responses to climate change remains challenging. The widely used space‐for‐time substitution (SFTS) approach assumes that ecological responses along spatial climate gradients can substitute for temporal relationships, yet agreement among spatial, temporal, and mechanistic approaches remains largely unknown. Using global satellite‐derived aboveground biomass (AGB) data, we quantified forest AGB sensitivities to spatial versus temporal climate variability, projected climate‐driven AGB changes under future emission scenarios, and compared results with Earth system models (ESMs). Spatial climate gradients explain substantially more AGB variation than temporal anomalies, with strong divergence across regions and forest ages. ESMs better reproduce spatial sensitivities than temporal ones. Temporal extrapolation generally projects future AGB gains, whereas spatial extrapolation often indicates AGB declines. These contrasts demonstrate that spatial, temporal, and model‐based approaches capture distinct facets of forest–climate coupling, and integrating them can better constrain uncertainty in carbon–climate feedbacks and improve future ecosystem projections.

title: Co‐producing urban silviculture: a stone soup approach to transdisciplinary science
content: On private or community land, urban forest patches are often overlooked but are critical green spaces that provide opportunities for transformative connections between humans and wild nature for local communities and ecosystems. Urban silviculture is an emergent land management practice that is best achieved as a transdisciplinary science, incorporating the knowledge and work of scientists, land managers, landscape designers, policymakers, and local residents to define problems, set long‐term goals, build partnerships, and realize solutions. The case study of Stillmeadow PeacePark, located on the grounds of Stillmeadow Community Fellowship church in Baltimore, Maryland, illustrates the potential for transdisciplinary co‐production of urban silviculture in the US and more broadly. This approach offers new insights into fundamental social–ecological processes and can address press and pulse disturbances at multiple scales. Developing community‐driven transdisciplinary science can be a way to create opportunities for restoration work in communities that have historically been excluded from financial investment and technical services.

title: Can killing individual wild animals directly protect their population?
content: Ongoing extinctions are often accelerated by humans intentionally killing nonhumans. Commonly in Western conservation thinking, killing is seen as a strategy to prevent extinction. The hypothesis that killing one animal can protect the survivors of the same species (conspecifics) requires a direct cause‐and‐effect mechanism between the death of the target and the outcomes or consequences for the surviving conspecifics. Otherwise, an indirect pathway with an additional step must be described and evaluated. We find rare direct (that is, one‐step) causal logic to support the “kill one to save many conspecifics” idea. Rare circumstances involve threats posed by the animal killed. To explore the more likely indirect (two‐step) causal logic, we describe the study designs needed for comparative evaluations of killing versus non‐lethal alternatives. For practitioners seeking science‐informed decisions, our analysis clearly indicates a gap in the available data and a narrow set of conditions in which one should “kill a few to save many conspecifics”.

title: Proton transport drives allosteric conformational changes in the MmpL3 transporter
content:
by Lixinhao Yang, E. Jeffrey North, Helen I. Zgurskaya, Mary Jackson, James C. Gumbart

Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains a global health crisis, further complicated by increasing drug resistance. The mycobacterial membrane protein MmpL3, which is essential for transporting cell wall precursors such as trehalose monomycolate (TMM), is a promising therapeutic target. However, the mechanistic link between proton-driven dynamics and substrate transport in MmpL3 is not fully understood. In this study, we use molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how protonation of conserved Asp-Tyr dyads (Asp256-Tyr646 and Asp645-Tyr257) in Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msmg) MmpL3 regulates conformational changes and TMM binding. Protonation at Asp256 induces an open dyad conformation, increases local water accessibility, and is associated with a tendency toward more open configurations of the periplasmic binding pocket. In contrast, protonation at Asp645 stabilizes a closed dyad conformation, reduces water accessibility, and narrows the transmembrane binding pocket. These findings support a proposed sequential protonation model in which protonation-dependent conformational changes are allosterically coupled to substrate translocation.

title: The successor representation in high-risk drinking and alcohol-related contexts
content:
by Milena Philomena Maria Musial, Sam Hall-McMaster, Kanji Shimomura, Ayaka Kato, Erik L. Bode, Clarissa C. Grundmann, Claudia Ebrahimi, Kenji Morita, Samuel J. Gershman, Tanja Endrass, Florian Schlagenhauf

The successor representation (SR) is a reinforcement learning strategy which has been suggested to underlie nuanced forms of habitual behavior, rendering it a candidate mechanism for mental health conditions thought to involve habitual control, such as addiction. However, paradigms used to assess habits in humans cannot detect SR use. Together with the fact that they are usually conducted in disorder-irrelevant contexts, this may explain why the evidence for a hypothesized shift from goal-directed to habitual behavior in addiction is inconsistent. Here, we tested whether individuals with high-risk (n = 260) compared to low-risk drinking behavior (n = 260) rely more on SR or a rigid goal-based dimension-reduced SR variant, particularly in alcohol-related contexts. An online multi-stage decision-making task performed in either a virtual bar or apartment context allowed us to dissociate (red)SR from model-based and model-free learning strategies by testing how well participants adapted their choices to different types of distal changes in the environment. Findings suggest that a particular type of SR, namely a (reduced) random-policy SR-like strategy, contributes to human behavior, but that high-risk drinkers do not differ from low-risk drinkers in their use of this strategy. Instead, both groups seem to rely less on what is likely a (reduced) random-policy SR strategy in alcohol-related contexts – and instead more on model-free control. Results suggest that the use of an adaptive, resource-efficient decision-making strategy is selectively downregulated in substance-related contexts. This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.

title: Spatio-temporal machine learning for multi-horizon prediction of bluetongue outbreaks
content:
by Lucy M. Devlin, Phi H. Nguyen, Ross N. Cuthbert, Phu Ngoc Doan, Viet Hung Tran, Zichi Zhang, Archie K. Murchie, Connor G. G. Bamford, Jaimie T. A. Dick, Eric R. Morgan, Thai S. Mai

Reliable early warning of infectious disease outbreaks remains a major challenge for surveillance systems, particularly for vector-borne pathogens whose transmission depends on interactions among hosts, vectors, and climate-sensitive environmental conditions. Data-driven forecasting offers a promising approach for predicting outbreak risk using surveillance and environmental data. This study develops a logit-weighted ensemble (LWE), a machine-learning framework that predicts outbreak occurrence 1–6 months ahead at the administrative unit–month scale using routinely available outbreak notifications and gridded climate data. Bluetongue virus (BTV), an arbovirus of ruminants transmitted by Culicoides biting midges, provides a well-characterised system in which transmission is strongly shaped by climate, making it a useful system for applying and testing this approach. The framework is evaluated using surveillance data collected between 2005 and 2024 from France, Greece, and Italy, selected for their long-running and high-quality outbreak surveillance records. Across all three countries, the LWE achieved the strongest and most stable predictive performance under a recall-focused evaluation that prioritises correctly identifying outbreak months. It outperformed or matched 14 benchmark models, with differences becoming more pronounced at longer lead times (month +3 onward), when predictions are more uncertain and outbreaks are relatively rare. Predictability varied across countries, with the highest performance in Greece, strong performance in France, and lower, more variable performance in Italy, reflecting differences in how consistently outbreaks occur and spread across regions. Overall, the results demonstrate that horizon-aware, climate-informed forecasting can reliably identify months and locations at elevated risk of outbreak occurrence up to six months in advance, supporting surveillance planning and preparedness across heterogeneous European settings. The ensemble framework provides a robust and portable strategy for outbreak prediction using routinely collected surveillance and environmental data.

title: SADRP: A structurally aware multi-modal framework for drug response prediction
content:
by Ren Qi, Shujia Liu, Tianhong Quan, Tianru Wu, Alexey K. Shaytan, Bin Liu

Motivation

Predicting drug sensitivity across diverse cancer samples is a fundamental challenge in personalized therapy and drug discovery. This task requires comprehensive characterization of both drug and cancer cell line features. Current approaches often fail to fully capture the complex structural characteristics and interactions of drug compounds and struggle to integrate multi-omics features derived from the same sample, limiting their feature representation capacity. Consequently, there is a need for modeling frameworks that can jointly model molecular structural features and multi-modal cellular contexts in a unified manner.

Results

We present SADRP, a structurally aware multi-modal framework for drug response prediction, designed to model complex molecular structures and multi-omics data. For drug representation, SADRP incorporates Shortest Distance Path (SDP) encoding and edge encoding to capture both topological relationships and bond-type chemical semantics. For cell line profiling, a multi-view interactive encoder integrates gene expression and DNA methylation, capturing cross-omics synergistic complementarity. SADRP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, while also identifying potential therapeutic candidates and biomarkers, providing mechanistic insights and supporting applications in drug discovery and personalized medicine.

title: Multiscale modeling reveals non-linear dynamics of AKT-mediated NO-ROS crosstalk in shear stress-induced endothelial phenotype
content:
by Yu-yuan Zhang, Yi-Teng Wang, Yan Qiu, Yong-Jiang Li, Dong Chen, Kai-Rong Qin

Endothelial dysfunction is a critical initiating event in atherosclerosis. The regulatory role of the AKT signaling pathway in the transition between injury and repair remains unclear. This study developed a multiscale model to elucidate how AKT signaling modulates endothelial repair under shear stress. The framework integrates hemodynamic stimuli, cellular behaviors, and nonlinear AKT/NO/ROS biochemical kinetics coupled with endothelial phenotypic transitions. Results demonstrate that endothelial dysfunction is driven by a spatial mismatch between NO production and ROS consumption rather than global deficiency. Phenotypic restoration is governed by the nonlinear interactions within the NO-ROS network. Systematic simulations identified a golden window, where Day 1 intervention and moderate AKT activation effectively restored endothelial cells and normalized redox status. Conversely, excessive activation caused supra-physiological over-suppression. These findings suggest that repair is determined by the tight coupling of redox homeostasis and immune dynamics, highlighting intervention timing and dosage as critical factors for precision vascular therapy.

title: Environmental volatility is associated with adaptive caution in visual search
content:
by Nan Qiu, Fredrik Allenmark, Siyi Chen, Hermann J. Müller, Zhuanghua Shi

Real-world distractors occur in environments whose states change at different rates. We asked whether such volatility alters initial overt oculomotor allocation, later target verification and response commitment, or both. Observers performed an additional-singleton search task with concurrent eye tracking while distractor presence followed high- or low-volatility sequences, with overall distractor prevalence held constant. Trial-pooled oculomotor capture was higher under high volatility, a pattern that appears to indicate altered filtering. Matching the same-location run position removed that difference, with no detectable difference in capture across volatility regimes at matched run position. The pooled capture effect was therefore consistent with a structural consequence of the volatility manipulation, which enriched high-volatility blocks with early-run positions where capture is intrinsically high. The volatility effect itself appeared on distractor-absent trials. Under high volatility, response times were longer, fixations more frequent, final-target dwell longer, and errors fewer, while target-acquisition latency itself was unchanged. Same-location repetition learning showed no detectable difference in slope across regimes. A hierarchical drift-diffusion model (DDM) and a complementary volatility Kalman-filter (VKF) comparison converged in showing that manual responses carried both boundary-related and drift-related structure. With distractor frequency held constant, the per-trial effect of volatility therefore emerged after the first saccade as an increase in response caution rather than in oculomotor capture. This pattern is consistent with precision-weighted adjustment to environmental uncertainty.

title: Non-adaptive evolutionary forces predominantly shape nucleotide composition near human transcription start sites
content:
by Yi Qiu, Emilie Hebraud, Fanny Pouyet, Alexander F. Palazzo

In the human genome, mutation rates vary along genes, yet how their fine-scale structure contributes to gene evolution has remained largely unexplored. Here, we map inherited mutations at single-nucleotide resolution and uncover a striking hypermutation peak at transcription start sites (TSSs) of human protein-coding genes. This pattern is observed both in population polymorphisms and in de novo mutations from parent-offspring trios, and is dependent on transcriptional activity in testes. We also find similar hypermutation peaks at TSSs used to produce long noncoding RNAs and at intergenic RNA Polymerase II pause sites. In addition, we identify distinct mutational signatures at exon-intron boundaries and in introns. By comparing the current nucleotide content to predicted equilibrium levels, inferred from mutation and fixation rates, and by analyzing derived ancestral frequency spectrums, we detect signals that are compatible with a low level of ongoing background GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC) throughout the region and ancestral elevated gBGC activity that is centered right downstream from the TSS. Using a forward-in-time simulation algorithm, we show that the current nucleotide composition surrounding the TSS of protein-coding genes is best explained by local mutation biases coupled to ongoing and ancestral patterns of gene conversions. Our simulations allow us to infer several features of these gBGC events. Overall, these findings indicate that the nucleotide composition around TSSs is largely shaped by non-adaptive forces, particularly mutation bias and gBGC.

title: A macrophage-targeted TIMD4 Peptide-Nanoparticle attenuates colitis symptoms and monocyte recruitment in a mouse model
content:
by Huimin Liu, Yuzhen Wang, Ruiqing Yu, Kexin Liu, Dezhi Zheng, Bo Wang, Yuan Chang, Bing Liu, Xuetian Yue, Zhuanchang Wu, Chunyang Li, Xiaohong Liang, Chunhong Ma, Guohua Liu, Jianhua Li, Leiqi Xu, Lifen Gao

Macrophages play a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain-containing molecule 4 (TIMD4) is involved in the regulation of tissue-resident macrophages. TIMD4 expression is elevated in colonic tissues from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and mice with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, but its role in IBD pathogenesis remains unclear. In this study, we found that Timd4 deficiency aggravated DSS-induced colitis, accompanied by increased infiltration of monocytes into the colonic tissues. Treatment with a CCR2 antagonist attenuated colonic inflammation and reduced monocyte infiltration into colonic tissues in Timd4 KO mice. Mechanistically, in vitro studies revealed that TIMD4 stabilized the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex via its intracellular domain, thereby activating the AMPK pathway and suppressing NF-κB-dependent chemokine production in macrophages. Based on these findings, we designed a TIMD4-derived peptide and developed a macrophage-targeted nanoparticle system (T4(365–378)‑NPs). Treatment with T4(365–378)-NPs reduced P65 phosphorylation and attenuated DSS-induced colitis in mice. Treatment with either T4(365–378)-NPs or the CCR2 antagonist attenuated DSS-induced colitis, and no statistically significant differences in the assessed outcomes were detected between the two groups. Administration of T4(365–378)-NPs before DSS exposure also attenuated subsequent colitis. Furthermore, combining the T4(365–378)‑NPs with anti-α4β7 or anti-TNF-α antibodies produced greater improvements than either monotherapy in the DSS-induced colitis model. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of TIMD4-derived peptide delivery as a potential therapeutic approach for intestinal inflammation.

title: Complementary stable and dynamic prelimbic ensembles encode learned threat value underlying generalization and discrimination
content: Adaptive behavior requires assigning emotional value to sensory cues and generalizing to similar stimuli. The prelimbic cortex (PL) is critical for threat expression and discrimination, yet its neuronal ensembles undergo substantial turnover over time. How stable population codes emerge despite this reorganization remains unknown. Using longitudinal calcium imaging in freely moving mice, we tracked PL activity for 30 days during auditory discriminative fear learning and retrieval. Despite substantial ensemble turnover, stable graded representations persisted in PL populations. A generalized linear model showed that the tone threat value explained graded activity better than freezing, indicating that PL primarily encodes stimulus significance. Population similarity across stimulus presentations was highest for shock-associated and highly generalized tones, suggesting a stable population code underlying threat generalization. Stable neurons preserved graded gradients across sessions, whereas learning modulated the rate of dynamic frequency-selective neurons. Together, these populations enabled stable threat-value coding despite ongoing ensemble reorganization.

title: Strong mnemonic prediction errors increase cognitive control, attention, and arousal
content: Ongoing experience is continuously processed in the context of past events. Divergence between current experience and memory-based predictions (i.e., a mnemonic prediction error; MPE) is theorized to be a signal that encoding, as opposed to retrieval, should be prioritized. We asked how MPEs place demands on control and attention-related processes, and whether these demands differ as a function of prediction strength. We investigated these questions across two experiments, wherein we recorded scalp electroencephalography and/or pupillometry as 101 young human adults performed an associative memory task. Strong MPEs, more so than weak MPEs, increased physiological indices of cognitive control (frontal theta), attention (posterior alpha and pupil size), and arousal (pupil size). Greater cognitive control (frontal theta) during strong MPEs promoted better learning of prediction-violating (i.e., unexpected) stimuli. Collectively, these findings reveal multiple pathways through which the mind and brain respond adaptively to violations of strong mnemonic predictions.

title: A mechanistic theory of planning in prefrontal cortex
content: Planning is critical for adaptive behaviour in a changing world, because it lets us anticipate the future and adjust our actions accordingly. While prefrontal cortex is crucial for this process, it remains unknown how planning is implemented in neural circuits. Prefrontal representations were recently discovered in simpler sequence memory tasks, where different populations of neurons represent different future time points. We demonstrate that combining such representations with the ubiquitous principle of neural attractor dynamics allows circuits to solve much richer problems, including planning. This is achieved by embedding the environment structure directly in synaptic connections to implement an attractor network that infers desirable futures. The resulting ‘spacetime attractor’ excels at planning in challenging tasks known to depend on the prefrontal cortex. Recurrent neural networks trained by gradient descent on such tasks learn a solution that precisely recapitulates the spacetime attractor – in representation, in dynamics, and in connectivity. Analyses of networks trained across different environment structures reveal a generalisation mechanism that rapidly reconfigures the world model used for planning, without the need for synaptic plasticity. The spacetime attractor is a testable mechanistic theory of planning. If true, it would provide a path towards detailed mechanistic understanding of how prefrontal cortex structures adaptive behaviour.

title: Net Carbon Transfer From Ocean to Land During the Last Deglaciation Synchronous With Sea Level Rise and Lagging Atmospheric CO2 by Several Millennia
content:
Abstract
The sequence of events in the global carbon cycle during deglaciations is not entirely understood. Here, we analyze mean ocean δ13 ${\delta }^{13}$C and δ18 ${\delta }^{18}$O in an updated compilation of foraminiferal stable isotope data comprising 902 time series from 381 sediment cores, with individual records covering intervals within the past 23,000 years. We use changes in mean ocean temperature from ice cores to split δ18 ${\delta }^{18}$O into its temperature and seawater components. We show that a 0.48±0.05 $0.48\pm 0.05$‰ rise in mean ocean δ13 ${\delta }^{13}$C occurred quasi‐synchronously with changes in seawater δ18 ${\delta }^{18}$O and is lagging the rise in atmospheric CO2 ${\mathrm{C}\mathrm{O}}_{2}$ during Termination I by ∼2,000 years. Since mean ocean δ13 ${\delta }^{13}$C is understood to mainly record net changes in land carbon storage and seawater δ18 ${\delta }^{18}$O is mainly depicting the rise in global mean sea level this implies that land carbon changed in‐phase with sea level and not with atmospheric CO2 ${\mathrm{C}\mathrm{O}}_{2}$.

title: A Radio Science Experiment for Dragonfly to Investigate Titan's Rotation and Interior Structure
content:
Abstract
NASA's mission Dragonfly to Titan is scheduled for launch in 2028 with arrival in 2034 to study Titan's prebiotic chemistry and habitability. We propose a radio science experiment for Dragonfly, in which radiometric tracking of the rotorcraft from the Deep Space Network, already baselined for communications and navigation, is used as a precision geodetic instrument to measure Titan's rotational state and tidal deformations, without any modification to the spacecraft. We perform simulations of the experiment and compute its expected performances in terms of the uncertainties on the retrieved geophysical parameters. Our results indicate that the rotation and tidal parameters can be retrieved with outstanding precision, sufficient to discriminate between models with and without a subsurface ocean, whose existence has been recently questioned. This experiment would be the first high‐precision geodetic experiment from a landed asset on an icy moon, and would provide dramatic improvements in our knowledge of Titan's interior.

title: Millennial‐Scale Climate States Alter Atlantic Multidecadal Variability Mechanisms in a Climate Model
content:
Abstract
The Atlantic Multidecadal Variability (AMV) influences North Atlantic sea surface temperatures and regional climate phenomena such as European droughts and hurricane activity. Its mechanisms remain complex due to long timescales and ocean‐atmosphere interactions. Here, we analyze a 2000‐year pre‐industrial climate model simulation revealing that millennial‐scale variability modulates AMV characteristics. During warm phases, the AMV is driven by a strong Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) and subsurface warming, indicating ocean circulation dominance. In cold phases, the AMV arises from atmospheric heat fluxes with surface‐confined warming and AMOC lagging AMV. These results demonstrate that millennial‐scale ocean variability influences AMV mechanisms and the AMV‐AMOC relationship, providing insights into North Atlantic climate variability and its potential predictability.
