title: Background Soil pH Governs Nitrogen‐Induced Acidification by Mediating Microbial N‐Cycling and Soil Buffering Capacity
content:
Abstract
Soil acidification caused by increased nitrogen (N) inputs has emerged as a global environmental concern that threatens ecosystem functioning and food security worldwide. However, how background soil pH influences the extent and mechanism of N‐induced acidification remains poorly understood. By assembling a global data set of field N addition experiments, we showed that the degree of acidification was most pronounced in neutral soils (pH 5.98–7.95), followed by acidic (pH ≤ 5.98) and alkaline (pH > 7.95) soils. In acidic soils, ammonia‐oxidizing archaea continuously released protons during the nitrification process, and the relatively weak buffering capacity exacerbated acidification. In neutral soils, N inputs increased the abundance of ammonia‐oxidizing bacteria (AOB) as well as nirS‐ and nirK‐harboring denitrifiers. These microbes exhibited strong N transformation capabilities, resulting in severe soil acidification due to the marked decline in buffering cations such as calcium (Ca2+) and magnesium (Mg2+). In alkaline soils, the high buffer capacity provided by carbonates (CO32−) initially mitigated acidification. However, high background pH promoted the growth of AOB and nirK denitrifiers after N inputs, potentially initiating acid‐generating reactions and gradually depleting the soil's CO32− buffer capacity. Our study suggests that N‐induced soil acidification is strongly regulated by background soil pH, with the microbial N transformation process and soil buffer capacity playing crucial mediating roles. These findings have important implications for developing sustainable soil management strategies under continued N enrichment.

title: Boundary Controls on Radium‐223 and Radium‐228 Distributions Along GEOTRACES GP17‐OCE: Implications for Trace Element Transport in the Distal South Pacific Ocean
content:
Abstract
In regions far removed from major atmospheric dust sources, such as the South Pacific and Southern Ocean, boundary exchange processes play a dominant role in regulating the supply of trace elements and their isotopes (TEIs) to the upper ocean, with important consequences for ecological stoichiometry and productivity. Here, we use radium (Ra) isotopes (223Ra, 226Ra, 228Ra) as tracers of boundary exchange along the US GEOTRACES GP17‐OCE Pacific and Southern Ocean transect, providing the first full ocean‐basin section of excess 223Ra. Activities of 228Ra exhibit a prominent subsurface maximum (mean ≈0.21 dpm/100 L) between 20°S and 55°S that persists to ≈800 m. Hydrographic context and GLORYS12 velocity fields link this maximum to Subantarctic Mode Water sourced over the shallow Campbell Plateau. We infer source activities of 0.22–0.31 dpm/100 L, implying ventilation and export on sub‐annual to 2‐year timescales. Near‐bottom inventories of 228Ra and excess 223Ra reveal spatially variable benthic fluxes, and zonal integration of 228Ra indicates that fluxes in the North and South Pacific are similar (2.8 × 1016 and 3.5 × 1016 dpm/yr, respectively), and comparable in magnitude to coastal 228Ra inputs to the Pacific Ocean. Above the Pacific–Antarctic Ridge, elevated excess 223Ra, 224Ra, and 228Ra, together with activity ratios, indicate entrainment of low‐temperature hydrothermal fluids that are weeks to a month old. Collectively, these results identify mode waters formed over the Campbell Plateau as a dominant conveyor of shelf‐derived Ra—and associated TEIs—to the South Pacific interior and document an active Pacific–Antarctic Ridge hydrothermal contribution that is underrepresented in current TEI models.

title: Contrasting isotopic responses of dryland and wetland plants to a century of global anthropogenic changes in nutrient cycling
content:
Contrasting isotopic responses of dryland and wetland plants to a century of global anthropogenic changes in nutrient cycling
Iwona Dembicz, Natalia Chojnowska, Piotr Chibowski, and Łukasz Kozub
Biogeosciences, 23, 7375–7396, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7375-2026, 2026
Plants from Polish wetlands and dry grasslands exhibit habitat-specific, century-scale shifts in carbon and nitrogen isotope signatures, as well as nitrogen concentrations. Wetlands exhibit stronger signals of human-driven alterations to the cycle of nutrients, probably linked to agricultural practices. Dry grasslands show smaller, atmosphere-driven changes. The effects of anthropogenic carbon and nitrogen on macronutrient cycling depend on habitat and species.

title: Hydrologic History Drives Divergent Soil Organic Matter Trajectories Across Hillslopes
content:
Abstract
Water availability governs soil organic matter (SOM) decomposition, yet how fine‐scale hydrologic variability shapes seasonal SOM processing and persistence remains unclear. In seasonally dry forests, rewetting can trigger rapid CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$ mineralization, but antecedent moisture may leave biogeochemical legacies that modulate this response and its significance for carbon and nutrient cycling. We examined whether subsurface water storage and antecedent moisture regulate SOM processing and carbon trajectories. We leveraged a natural gradient in plant‐accessible water across two Douglas‐fir‐dominated hillslopes in Oregon's western Cascade Mountains (USA). These sites experience similar climate, vegetation, and soils, but differ in subsurface water‐storage capacity. We compared dry‐season (June) soils with wet‐season (December) soils, and paired continuous soil‐moisture profiles with high‐resolution mass spectrometry of water‐extractable (WEOM) and mineral‐associated organic matter (MAOM), bulk SOM pools, and microbial‐biomass. SOM chemistry was similar in June but diverged in hillslope‐specific ways by December. Soils from the high‐water‐storage hillslope accumulated OM in WEOM and MAOM and gained microbial biomass carbon, shifting toward more oxidized, relatively complex compounds. Soils from the low‐water‐storage hillslope lost OM across fractions and microbial biomass carbon, and retained more reduced, relatively simple compounds. High‐water‐storage profiles remained within 50−70% $50-70\%$ water‐holding capacity longer—an optimum for microbial activity—whereas low‐water‐storage sites dried faster and experienced larger moisture extremes. Plant‐mediated hydraulic redistribution occurred on both hillslopes, but was not a key mechanism maintaining optimal soil water‐holding capacity. These insights support a hillslope storage framework: subsurface storage can imprint biogeochemical legacies of moisture conditions, shaping decomposer responses to cool‐season wetting in seasonally dry landscapes.

title: Submesoscale Frontogenesis Drives Strong Finescale Tracer Subduction
content:
Abstract
Vertical exchange between the surface mixed layer (ML) and the interior is important for biogeochemistry and air–sea interaction. Focused observations have consistently shown that submesoscale processes (horizontal scales of 0.1–10 km) generate substantial exchange of heat, freshwater, and biogeochemical tracers across the ML base, particularly near fronts. However, the role of finescale turbulence in this exchange remains poorly understood. Here we investigate this multiscale problem by analyzing the transport of a surface‐fluxed passive tracer in large‐eddy simulations of baroclinic mixed‐layer instabilities (MLIs) under surface cooling. Budgets for the tracer below the evolving ML show that finescale turbulence contributes to tracer subduction only at fronts sharpened to a few hundred meters wide by eddy straining and horizontal convergence. Although submesoscale vertical flux dominates the exchange across the ML base, finescale turbulent flux is comparable to the indirect contribution from MLI‐induced restratification. Analysis of the finescale energetics shows that the turbulence at sharp fronts is primarily driven by shear production associated with frontogenesis, with large contributions from horizontal shear, rather than by convective forcing. In contrast, outside the frontal zone turbulence is driven solely by surface forcing, and the tracer is largely confined to the ML. This suggests a multiscale picture of vertical exchange at submesoscale fronts that is not represented in existing parameterizations. Submesoscale‐permitting ocean models may partially capture the frontogenetic process, but the associated forward energy flux is likely dissipated implicitly or explicitly, rather than contributing to vertical mixing and tracer transport.

title: In Subtropical Western North Pacific Typhoons, Prior Along‐Track Marine Heatwave Contact Is Associated With Rapid Intensification
content:
Abstract
Annual marine heatwave (MHW) days more than tripled in the subtropical western North Pacific between 1982–2002 and 2003–2023. Previous studies mainly examined concurrent MHW conditions, often using coarser‐resolution sea surface temperature (SST) analyses. Less attention has been given to MHW exposure earlier along individual storm tracks before rapid intensification (RI, ≥ ${\ge} $30 kt strengthening in 24 hr). Using a storm‐specific anchor, we matched Digital Typhoon tracks to longer‐record and higher‐resolution daily SST analyses. In the longer record, RI occurred in 9.09% of storms with prior contact and 3.52% without it. The adjusted odds ratio was 2.72 after accounting for storm intensity, motion, duration, genesis location, year, and season. In the higher‐resolution analysis, RI occurred in 12.24% of storms with prior contact and 4.59% without it, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.36. The association remained positive after environmental controls and across RI‐threshold and bathymetric sensitivities, but was weaker and statistically uncertain in the low‐latitude subdomain. Among RI storms with prior contact, median maximum MHW event duration was 25.5 days in the longer‐record analysis and 17 days in the higher‐resolution analysis, while median cumulative storm contact lasted 14.5 and 7 hr, respectively. First contact preceded RI by a median of 38–42 hr. Detrended and moving‐baseline MHW definitions gave weaker, uncertain estimates of 1.84 and 1.51. Across both analyses, RI probability was highest after prior MHW contact, while storms encountering positive SST anomalies that did not meet the MHW criterion showed less consistent differences from neutral conditions.

title: Characteristics of Interfacial Waves Over a Liquefied Seabed and Their Effects on Sediment Suspension
content:
Abstract
Wave‐induced seabed liquefaction can enhance coastal sediment suspension, but the wave‐cycle‐scale influence of interfacial‐wave motion remains poorly understood. Wave‐flume experiments were conducted on a silty bed under two regular‐wave conditions to compare near‐bed hydrodynamics and sediment suspension between a non‐liquefied condition and a liquefied condition. Under the non‐liquefied condition, suspended sediment concentration (SSC) exhibited a double‐peaked intra‐wave pattern and generally varied with turbulent kinetic energy and Reynolds shear stress, suggesting predominantly shear‐related suspension. After liquefaction, sustained interfacial waves developed at the mudline, with a root‐mean‐square amplitude of approximately 1.4 cm. Around the onset of sustained interfacial‐wave motion, near‐bed SSC increased from approximately 1.3 to 2.6 g L−1 within 4–5 wave cycles, the intra‐wave SSC distribution shifted to a single‐peaked pattern, and its relationship with Reynolds shear stress weakened. During rapid mudline descent, upward turbulent sediment transport was strongest and accounted for approximately 93% of the positive cycle‐integrated turbulent sediment flux. Under the experimental conditions examined, these observations suggest that interfacial‐wave motion may provide an additional phase‐dependent mechanism modulating sediment suspension over a liquefied seabed, offering a physical basis for improving the representation of sediment transport over liquefied beds.

title: Cryptic Diversity and Patterns of Structure in Nine Species of North Pacific Rockfishes (Sebastes spp. and Sebastolobus spp.)
content:
ABSTRACT
Understanding how habitat and life history traits contribute to population genetic structure is critical for evaluating conservation risks and identifying optimal management of wild populations. Species derived from adaptive radiations can provide a useful model for studying such patterns because the presence of some consistent traits allows for closer examination of attributes which differ. Here, we examine population structure in rockfishes (genera Sebastes and Sebastolobus), a group of speciose, recently diverged marine fishes that exhibit a continuum of genetic structure, from cryptic species to putative genetic panmixia. In this study, we analyse low‐coverage whole genome resequencing data from nine rockfish species and identify four major types of genetic differentiation: cryptic diversity, isolation‐by‐distance (IBD), no detectable structure (putative panmixia) and no detectable structure with a single genomic region putatively underlying local adaptation. Two species, Dark (Sebastes ciliatus) and Northern (S. polyspinis) rockfishes, each exhibited cryptic diversity consisting of two sympatric groups differentiated at every chromosome throughout the genome. Black rockfish in Southeast Alaska also had two genetic groups, despite an overall signal of IBD from the West Coast of North America through the Gulf of Alaska (GOA). Five species showed evidence of genetic panmixia throughout the sampled range, while Yelloweye Rockfish exhibited high gene flow across ~4000 km, from southern California to the GOA, but had strong differentiation between the Salish Sea and the outer coast. Of the species in which no structure was detected, only Blackspotted Rockfish had one outlier region exhibiting signatures of potential local adaptation. Our results highlight how multiple mechanisms likely promote genetic structure in rockfishes, hinting at tentative links to depth distributions and offshore habitats that might influence patterns of differentiation in rockfishes more broadly. Further, this study provides genetic data for some of the most abundant rockfishes in commercial fisheries in the Northeast Pacific, enhancing the scientific information available for informing fisheries management.

title: Independent Major‐Effect Loci and Limited Trait Associations Characterize Warning Colour Variation Across Sexes and Life Stages in the Wood Tiger Moth (Arctia plantaginis)
content:
ABSTRACT
Variation in warning colouration is common, despite strong positive frequency‐dependent selection favouring the most common morph and may arise from spatially or temporally variable selection or associations with other traits. We investigated the maintenance of warning colour variation in the wood tiger moth, Arctia plantaginis, which shows sexual dimorphism in colouration: two distinct male morphs controlled by a single locus, and continuous variation in female hindwing colour and larval warning signal size. Using whole‐genome sequencing of 657 individuals from a laboratory stock derived from a wild polymorphic population, we examined the genetic basis of multiple life‐history traits, chemical defence, pheromones and male activity. We specifically tested for associations with male colour and aimed to identify the genetic basis of female and larval colour variation. We detected separate major‐effect loci for female colour and larval signal size, which were different from the male colour locus. Hindwing melanism was the only trait associated with male colour, mapping to a nearby major‐effect locus and showing a link to reduced activity at higher temperatures. Female colour was phenotypically correlated with pheromone amount. However, apart from melanism, none of the traits measured showed an association with any of the loci controlling warning colours and we found no evidence that male colour is part of a ‘supergene’ or complex co‐adapted phenotype. Instead, our results indicate largely independent genetic architectures for warning colours, suggesting that variable selection rather than genetic associations may contribute to the maintenance of colour polymorphisms in this species.

title: Novel use of ink by territorial males in the coastal squid Heterololigo bleekeri
Improving island occupancy predictions using ecologically informed metrics of area and isolation
content:
Abstract
Understanding how species occupy islands and habitat patches remains a central question in biogeography, landscape ecology, conservation, and management, especially as natural and anthropogenic processes reconfigure habitat size and connectivity over time. The insular distribution function (IDF) provides a framework for predicting occupancy patterns for a species based on island area and isolation as proxies for extinction risk and colonization likelihood. While this model provides a conceptual bridge between island biogeography and metapopulation models, it has seen limited recent application in large part due to reliance on simplistic geometric measures of area and isolation. Here, we advance the implementation of the IDF by pulling from ecological niche modeling and landscape ecology to incorporate ecologically informed quantifications of area and isolation. We apply this framework to the montane sky‐islands of the Great Basin of the western United States, testing predictions for the Western Water Shrew (Sorex navigator). Compared with those based on traditional geometric metrics, the ecologically informed IDFs produced a discriminant function with lower classification error, stronger class separation, and different biological conclusions regarding the species' inferred response to isolation and area. The results from the ecologically informed IDF provide a contrast to IDF based on geographic axes and the classical interpretations for the system. Specifically, the steeper slope and lower intercept of the ecologically informed IDF point toward a system structured not so strongly by extinction‐driven relaxation, but by a more compensatory trade‐off in which both colonization and extinction have shaped occupancy patterns. Simulations of false‐absence rates (which affect datasets in lesser‐sampled systems) showed that the same inferences persisted in the presence of incomplete sampling. These results highlight the potential of integrating contemporary approaches with classic biogeographic models, as well as strengthening and clarifying links between island biogeography and landscape ecology. This updated analytical framework offers new opportunities for assessing subpopulation vulnerability, incorporating ecologically informed measures into occupancy‐based statistical frameworks, forecasting patchy species distributions across a full community, and studying how past and future environmental changes shape biodiversity patterns.

title: Net ecosystem productivity of grasslands: A chamber‐based global database
content:
Abstract
Net ecosystem productivity (NEP) of global grasslands—one of the largest and most variable components of the terrestrial carbon budget—provides critical insight into the magnitude and dynamics of the global carbon balance. Extensive field measurements have been derived from static‐chamber techniques; however, these data have remained fragmented at individual sites or regions and have seldom been synthesized into a consistent global product. Here, chamber‐based NEP measurements from 221 publications (1992–2023) in global grasslands were obtained, critically filtered, and condensed in a comprehensive global database. This database comprised 1521 individual NEP records from 275 sites across 30 countries. The dataset further included information on site location, ecosystem type, dominant species, climatic variables, soil properties, measurement timing (year, month, and day), and sampling protocol. The study sites encompassed global grasslands with latitudinal range of 62.22° S to 78.88° N, longitudinal range of 156.62° W to 161.51° E, and altitudes from −1 to 4852 m above sea level, covering broad climatic gradients (mean annual temperature: −17°C to 32.1°C; mean annual precipitation: 17–2226 mm; potential evapotranspiration: 152–1819 mm year−1). Our database enables (1) elucidation of the biogeographic pattern of grassland NEP, (2) assessment of grassland carbon‐sequestration potential under future global‐change scenarios, and (3) validation of both machine‐learning and process‐based model estimates of grassland NEP at the global scale. The database is available under a CC BY 4.0 license. The authors kindly request users to cite this data paper while using the database in acknowledgment of all the hard work that went into compiling the data.

title: Eco‐Evolutionary Feedback to a Pesticide Worsens the Impact of a Pesticide Switch in a Pivotal Freshwater Non‐Target Species
content:
Selection under the insecticide chlorpyrifos strongly affected the genetic makeup of non‐target Daphnia magna populations and increased tolerance of chlorpyrifos‐selected populations to chlorpyrifos and malathion (same mode of action as chlorpyrifos) but reduced performance when exposed to deltamethrin (different mode of action from chlorpyrifos). The findings reveal eco‐evolutionary trade‐offs that may increase vulnerability under pesticide rotation practices.

ABSTRACT
Pest management often requires the rotation of insecticides, sequentially exposing non‐target populations to different compounds. In a two‐phased experiment, we assessed whether exposure to the pesticide chlorpyrifos induces rapid evolution in the non‐target species Daphnia magna and quantified the response of control and pre‐exposed populations to a second exposure to the same pesticide, another pesticide with the same mode of action (malathion), or a pesticide with another mode of action (deltamethrin). Chlorpyrifos selection induced rapid shifts in genotype composition and reduced genotype richness and strongly influenced population development following the second exposure. Chlorpyrifos‐selected populations outperformed control populations when subsequently exposed to chlorpyrifos and malathion but underperformed when exposed to deltamethrin. Our results highlight an eco‐evolutionary feedback in which rapid adaptive responses to a pesticide worsen the response when exposed to a different type of pesticide in non‐target species, increasing vulnerability to common agricultural practices.

title: Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation
content:
by Susanne Dahle, Gaute T. Einevoll, Torbjørn V. Ness

There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. This has made it difficult to obtain general insights into how tES modulates neural activity, and a central challenge lies in the cell-type-specific and frequency-dependent nature of these responses. In this study, we investigated cell-type-specific neuronal responses to tES over a broad frequency range, using a large database of biophysically detailed neuron models. We found that pyramidal cells respond strongly to low-frequency tES, but their responses drop sharply with frequency. In contrast, inhibitory neurons show a smaller reduction and, on average, become more responsive than pyramidal cells above ~60 Hz. By leveraging a reciprocity theorem we demonstrated that the effect of tES on a given cell-type is proportional to the frequency-dependent current-dipole moment that determines the EEG-signal contribution of this cell-type. We further identified the dendritic asymmetry as key in determining tES responses across the frequency spectrum. Counterintuitively, we also found that while total cell length increases tES sensitivity at low frequencies, it can have the opposite effect at high frequencies. Furthermore, we derived an analytical formula for idealized neuron models which can approximately predict the tES sensitivity of different cell types at any given frequency. By characterizing the role of morphology and stimulation frequency in determining tES responses of single cells, this is an important step towards a better understanding of tES at the fundamental level. These results also provide an efficient and accurate method for characterizing and comparing the tES responses of different neural populations across the frequency spectrum, which facilitates optimizing tES for cell-type specific targeting.

title: Ten simple rules for responsible use of AI and LLMs in computational biology
content: by Noam Auslander

title: The evolutionary accessibility of cultural fitness landscapes
content:
by Laurel Fogarty, Rebecca B. Hoyle

Many human cultural and technological traits have a complex and peculiar structure. They are often characterized by multiple closely interacting parts that can form modules, and change as a result of innovation, collaboration, and social learning. A full understanding of the ways in which such cultural traits evolve requires a model that accounts for the close epistatic interaction of the constituent parts, and for the uniquely cultural processes that act on them. Here, we generalize the concept of ‘adaptive landscapes’, where populations search a landscape for optimal combinations of components. This generalization accounts for epistatic interactions, and includes processes such as modularization, communication, and collaboration, that are not features of genetic systems but may be quite common features of cultural systems. We show that modularization in combination with collaborative communication of search results is more successful, but sometimes more costly, than searching a full adaptive landscape. However, in many of the circumstances under which technology evolves, a full search of many thousands of possible modules may not be feasible since time, financial, energetic, and environmental constraints are likely to be strong. Under these conditions, our models suggest that there is a critical value for the number of modules to search below which the global optimum is more likely to be reached by searching the full landscape. The value of this threshold depends on the complexity of the technology. Overall, we suggest that analysis of cultural fitness landscapes is likely to be a fruitful avenue for research into technological change especially when combined with elements of human learning and interaction known to be important features of cultural evolution.

title: Host–virus interactions dominate fitness and conceal additive genetic variation
content:
by Aleksei Belyi, Yiyang Du, Alastair J. Wilson, Ben Longdon, Francis M. Jiggins

Host–parasite coevolution is expected to generate strong selection for resistance and infectivity that has the potential to erode genetic variation. Despite this, natural populations often retain extensive genetic variation in these traits. Genotype-by-genotype interactions on fitness can generate negative frequency-dependent selection, which helps maintain this variation by preventing any host or pathogen genotype from retaining a permanent advantage. Because these interactions place genetic variance in the interaction term rather than in additive differences among hosts or pathogens, that variance is masked from directional selection and can remain ‘cryptic’. Here we combine coevolutionary modelling with large‑scale experimental infection assays to quantify how host-pathogen interactions structure fitness variance in a vertically transmitted virus system, Drosophila melanogaster and sigma virus. Simulations show that coevolution typically erodes additive genetic variance in host and pathogen fitness, concentrating variance in host-virus interaction terms. Consistent with these predictions, experiments spanning 90 host-virus genotype combinations reveal that transmission, viral load, and virulence are overwhelmingly governed by host-virus genetic interactions rather than host or virus main effects. As a result, neither host resistance alleles nor viral genotypes confer consistently higher fitness across genetic backgrounds. Interactions tend to be sex‑specific, further limiting heritable fitness variation. Our results demonstrate that coevolution can substantially mask heritable genetic variation from directional selection by rendering fitness context-dependent. This extensive cryptic genetic variation may be revealed either when ecological or evolutionary conditions shift, or when the process of coevolution itself alters the direction of selection. This demonstrates the need to account for genotype-specific interactions when forecasting evolutionary responses.

title: A cortical semantic map integrates fractions and integers in the human brain
content:
by Daniela Valério, Samuel Debray, Alireza Karami, Maxime Cauté, Nicolás Gravel, Stanislas Dehaene

How does the human brain represent the meaning of abstract symbols? Some theories postulate the existence of semantic spaces where concepts occupy positions that reflect their conceptual relationships. In the number domain, psychological evidence suggests that integers are represented along a mental number line which, with education, integrates higher-level number concepts such as fractions. To test this hypothesis, we recorded whole-brain 7T fMRI responses to integer and fraction symbols during an active magnitude comparison task designed to engage magnitude processing. Consistent with predictions, we found both behavioral and neural numerical distance effects. Activation vectors in intraparietal, inferior temporal, prefrontal, hippocampal, and parahippocampal cortices formed a two-dimensional semantic space organized by numerical magnitude and domain (fractions versus integers). Gaussian fits revealed a topographic map of numerical preferences in the anterior inferior parietal cortex, common to both domains. Our results suggest that, when educated adults engage in an explicit magnitude comparison task, their brain can construct an ordered representation that integrates fractions and integers, with a topographic organization in the anterior IPS/IPL.

title: Olfactory combinatorial coding supports risk–reward decision-making in Caenorhabditis elegans
content: Olfactory-driven behaviors are essential for animal survival, but mechanisms for decoding olfactory inputs remain poorly understood. We have used whole-network Ca2+ imaging to study olfactory coding in Caenorhabditis elegans. We show that the odorant 1-octanol is encoded combinatorially in the periphery as both an attractant and a repellent. These inputs are integrated centrally, and their relative strengths determine the sensitivity and valence of the behavioral response through modulation of locomotory reversals and speed. The balance of these pathways also dictates the activity of the locomotory command interneurons, which control locomotory reversals. This balance serves as a regulatory node for response modulation, allowing C. elegans to weigh opportunities and hazards in its environment when formulating behavioral responses. Thus, an odorant can be encoded simultaneously as inputs of opposite valence, focusing attention on the integration of these inputs in determining perception, response, and plasticity.

title: Motor unit mechanisms of speed control in mouse locomotion
content: During locomotion, the coordinated activity of dozens of muscles shapes the kinematic features of each stride, including systematic changes in limb movement across walking speed. Motor units, each of which consists of a single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates, contribute to the total activation of each muscle through their recruitment and firing rate when active. However, it remains unknown how the nervous system controls locomotor speed by changing the firing of individual motor units. To address this, we combined quantitative behavioral analysis of mouse locomotion with single motor unit recordings from the lateral and long heads of the triceps brachii, which drive monoarticular extension of the elbow and biarticular movements of the elbow and shoulder, respectively. In contrast to prior studies employing bulk electromyography (EMG) to examine muscle activity, our recordings revealed the diversity of spike patterning across motor units, as well as systematic differences in motor unit activity across muscles and locomotor speeds. First, motor unit activity differed significantly across the lateral and long heads, suggesting differential control of these two closely apposed elbow extensor muscles. Second, we found that individual units were recruited probabilistically (during only a subset of strides), showing that the highly repeatable bulk EMG signals observed across strides, in fact, reflect varying subsets of individual motor units. Finally, although recruitment probability and firing rate both increased at faster walking speeds, increases in recruitment were proportionally larger than rate changes, and recruitment of individual units accompanied changes in limb kinematics. Together, these results reveal how the firing of individual motor units varies systematically across muscles and walking speeds to produce flexible locomotor behavior.

title: Seasonal Variations of the Martian Middle‐Atmosphere CO2/Ar Ratio Inferred From MAVEN/NGIMS Observations
content:
Abstract
The carbon dioxide (CO2)/argon (Ar) ratio is a useful tracer of atmospheric circulation on Mars, but it remains observationally poorly constrained in the middle atmosphere, where large‐scale circulation occurs. In this study, we infer the CO2/Ar ratio at the homopause, which marks the upper boundary of the well‐mixed Martian middle atmosphere, by extrapolating observations from NASA’s Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN mission. The inferred ratio shows a double‐peaked seasonal variation, with minima near equinoxes and maxima near solstices, broadly consistent with simulations from a Mars General Circulation Model (GCM). However, we also identify pronounced high‐latitude enhancements of this ratio during LS ∼ 270°–300°, reaching ∼80–110 compared with ∼60 predicted by the GCM. These enhancements may indicate a transient atmospheric circulation pattern not captured by the model simulations. Our results provide a new observational constraint on composition near the Martian homopause and, consequently, on middle‐atmosphere circulation, and suggest that additional atmospheric processes remain to be understood.

title: Rapid Infiltration Signatures From Global Infiltration Observations
content:
Abstract
Rapid infiltration influences rainfall partitioning, subsurface water movement, and freshwater availability, yet its large‐scale spatial organization remains poorly constrained by limited observations and the lack of scalable approaches for synthesizing infiltration measurements. Here, we identify rapid infiltration signatures from a global database using a dual‐mechanism modeling framework. Rapid infiltration signatures occurred in 26.6% of 4,992 valid curves. Occurrence varied among measurement methods, while rapid and non‐rapid signatures frequently coexisted within closely matched local contexts. At identical recorded locations, 74.7% of qualifying groups contained both rapid and non‐rapid signatures; for rapid‐classified curves, the fitted rapid component accounted for a median 41.2% of cumulative infiltration. Across 83 sites, rapid‐signature odds decreased by approximately 26% per 10° increase in absolute latitude. These findings provide a large‐scale observational basis for investigating rapid infiltration and highlight the importance of measurement context and independent physical evidence for improving its representation in hydrological and Earth system models.

title: Interhemispheric Stratospheric Symmetry: Seasonal Precursors to Surface Extratropical Variability
content:
Abstract
Seasonal prediction of surface climate relies on influences external to the troposphere, of which the stratosphere is a key source. The October stratosphere is particularly important for predictability of the coming winter and summer seasons in the Northern and Southern Hemisphere respectively, as the seasonal transition in zonal winds creates an interhemispherically symmetric window of stratosphere‐troposphere coupling. Building on a recently identified teleconnection between the October upper stratospheric meridional wind and the December‐January‐February (DJF) North Atlantic Oscillation, we use reanalysis to demonstrate an analogous Southern Hemisphere teleconnection predicting the DJF Southern Annular Mode with skill (r=0.53) $(r=0.53)$ comparable to current operational seasonal forecasts. We show that CMIP6 models fail to capture either teleconnection and that model skill is contingent on representation of the stratospheric pathway connecting the October meridional wind indices to the respective DJF polar vortex, a relationship that is poorly captured across models in both hemispheres.

title: Acoustic‐Seismic Coupling Signals From Aircraft Reveal Firn‐Ice Transition and Near‐Surface Elastic Structure of Antarctic Ice
content:
Abstract
Predicting the response of Antarctic ice to climate change requires detailed knowledge of its shallow structure, but direct measurements are challenging. Traditional seismic surveys are logistically demanding, and surface remote sensing provides limited information about subsurface layers. Here, we introduce uncontacted airborne seismology, a method that uses aircraft‐generated sounds and their conversion into seismic waves at the ice surface to probe the ice interior. Using a 36‐node seismic array during airborne passes, we captured multiple types of seismic waves and analyzed their propagation to extract dispersion patterns. Joint inversion of these observations reconstructs the elastic properties and porosity of the upper ∼100 m. This approach offers a rapid, scalable framework for mapping near‐surface ice structure and establishes a benchmark for future aerial or robotic exploration of polar regions, opening new possibilities for large‐scale, noninvasive monitoring of ice sheet dynamics.

title: Cessation of Nearby Low‐Frequency Earthquake Activity Following the December 2024 Mw 7.0 Mendocino Earthquake: The Likely Role of Pore Pressure Reductions
content:
Abstract
Earthquakes affect surrounding fault systems through multiple mechanisms. Here, we examine a rare cessation of activity in 27 families of low‐frequency earthquakes (LFEs) that likely reflect fault creep at the southern edge of Cascadia subduction, near the Mendocino triple junction. These sources usually exhibit nearly daily activity but were shut off for ∼7–25 days following the December 2024 moment magnitude (Mw) 7.0 Mendocino fault earthquake. Based on modeling, we infer that this cessation was not caused by induced shear stress, which was slightly encouraging of slip, but rather by combined clamping normal stress and reduced pore pressure. This mechanism, which isn't captured in the common effective friction simplification, may have strengthened the fault and inhibited creep, without requiring fluid outflow. Observed variations in LFE cessation times are not predicted by modeled stress changes alone and may instead reflect differing source dimensions or subtle variations in LFE fault geometry.

title: Revealing the Hydrothermal System of La Soufrière Volcano (Guadeloupe) Through Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography
content:
Abstract
La Soufri'ere de Guadeloupe is an active volcano of the Lesser Antilles Volcanic Arc. Its last eruption halted in 1977, yet hydrothermal activity has increased over recent years, raising summit instability hazards. The link between hydrothermal fluids and detachment landslide surfaces is well established and exacerbated by inflation, pressurization, and fluid flow lubrication. Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography offers the resolution and penetration needed to investigate such features in 3D. In 2023, we deployed 39 nodal geophones that recorded for about 1 month. The resulting 3D S‐wave velocity model resolves a central low‐velocity conduit, possible flank detachment planes, and subsurface structures of the shallow volcanic cone. Our results highlight the complex interaction between fluid transport (meteoric and magmatic) and tectono‐magmatic drivers. This provides the first high‐resolution 3D seismic imaging for slope stability assessment in volcanic environments. Understanding detachment zone geometry and distribution contributes to hazard risk assessment and mitigation.

title: Observing Methane Emissions From Oil and Gas Infrastructure in the Permian Basin Using TROPOMI
content:
Abstract
The Permian Basin is one of the largest methane sources in the United States, yet quantifying emissions at scales needed to attribute them to specific infrastructure remains challenging. Here we present a methane flux inversion from 2018 through 2025 using TROPOMI retrievals and a machine learning surrogate for atmospheric transport (FootNet). We estimate emissions at 1 × 1 km2 ${\text{km}}^{2}$ spatial resolution and weekly time resolution over the Permian Basin, jointly solving for background concentrations. We find total Permian Basin emissions of 2.6 ± $\pm $ 0.5 Tg/yr (structural uncertainty range: 1.7–3.2 Tg/yr), a factor of 2.4 higher than the EPA inventory, with strong spatial correspondence to gas wells, pipelines, storage tanks, compressor stations, and processing facilities. Permian sub‐basins have distinct drivers of methane emissions: gas wells in the Delaware, midstream infrastructure in the Midland. Despite a 2–3× increase in production, total emissions remained stable, driving a decline in methane intensity from 5% to 2%.
