title: Fine-scale spatial variability of winter CO2 and CH4 fluxes in Arctic tundra derived from snowpack gradient measurements
content:
Fine-scale spatial variability of winter CO2 and CH4 fluxes in Arctic tundra derived from snowpack gradient measurements
Gabriel Hould Gosselin, Nick Rutter, Paul J. Mann, Philip Marsh, and Oliver Sonnentag
Biogeosciences, 23, 7447–7467, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7447-2026, 2026
We studied how Arctic tundra soils exchange carbon dioxide and methane with the atmosphere during winter in the western Canadian Arctic. Using gas concentration profiles through the snow, we quantified greenhouse gas fluxes and their spatial variability across vegetation and terrain types. Carbon dioxide emissions increased with deeper snow and warmer soils, while some areas absorbed methane. These findings provide key data to improve upscaling of winter carbon fluxes across Arctic landscapes.

title: Timing of the anthropogenic carbon invasion  in the Southern California Current
content:
Timing of the anthropogenic carbon invasion in the Southern California Current
Yéssica Vanessa Contreras-Pacheco, Jose Luis Abella-Gutiérrez, Gerardo Vallejo-Espinosa, and Juan Carlos Herguera-García
Biogeosciences, 23, 7397–7409, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7397-2026, 2026
In the southern California Current, seasonal winds bring nutrient-rich waters to the surface, influencing local carbon levels. By analyzing ~ 160 years of sediment records, we reveal long-term shifts in carbon patterns that reflect both human-driven changes in the atmosphere and natural ocean mixing. These findings improve our understanding of how highly productive coastal regions contribute to the global carbon cycle.

title: Human and climate-environment interactions in Pyrenean landscapes: a Lateglacial-Holocene multiproxy reconstruction
content:
Human and climate-environment interactions in Pyrenean landscapes: a Lateglacial-Holocene multiproxy reconstruction
Irene Julián-Posada, Graciela Gil-Romera, Ana Moreno, Bérangère Leys, Blas Valero-Garcés, and Penélope González-Sampériz
Biogeosciences, 23, 7411–7446, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7411-2026, 2026
The subalpine belt of the Pyrenees, once forested, is now a mosaic of forest patches and open landscapes with pastures. We reconstruct the palaeoenvironmental history using sedimentary ancient DNA, pollen and charcoal. We show that Neoglacial cooling initially opened the forest, and pastoralism through fire and grazing maintained it. These landscapes result not from climate or humans alone, but from their long-term synergy, implying that conservation must emulate traditional herding practices.

title: Dynamics of Rainfall‐NDVI Relationships: Testing the Pulse‐Reserve and Two‐Layer Hypotheses
content:
Abstract
Water availability significantly affects vegetation in dry regions. We studied how Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) relates to rainfall pulses, or soil water reservoirs, across three continents: Australia, North America, and the Middle East, from 2011 to 2022. High‐resolution satellite images, at daily and tens‐of‐meters scales, were used to compute NDVI for four vegetation formations: herbaceous vegetation, shrubs, forest, and wheat fields, alongside corresponding daily rainfall data. First, we determined the minimal representative area for these vegetation formations and study sites. We found that this area ranged 0.02–0.14 km2 ${\text{km}}^{2}$, with variation depending more on vegetation formation than on geographic location. Second, our results, across soil texture, continents, climate conditions, and vegetation formations, challenge the Pulse‐Reserve hypothesis while supporting Walter's Two‐Layer hypothesis. Our results show that shallow‐rooted vegetation responds to ∼3‐month and deep‐rooted vegetation to ∼1‐year rainfall accumulation. These findings emphasize the importance of long‐term water storage rather than immediate rainfall pulses in semiarid ecosystems.

title: Transposable Element Activity Is Associated With the Rise of Termite Diversity
content:
ABSTRACT
Transposable elements (TEs) have long been hypothesized as a driver of lineage diversification due to their mutagenic ability. However, the correlation between rates of TE activity and diversification has rarely been tested, since it is challenging to measure the rate of TE activity in the deep past. Here, we investigated TE activity during the last ~150 million years of termite evolution. First, we determined the timing of TE amplification events using the sequence divergence of TE copies and identified two waves of TE bursts that took place synchronously across termite lineages, coinciding with the two major phases of termite diversification. Furthermore, we built phylogenetic trees using the presence/absence of orthologous TE insertions in the flanking regions of Ultraconserved Elements (UCEs), in which the branch length provided a measure of the rate of TE insertion/deletion near UCEs along the termite phylogenetic tree. The rate of TE insertion/deletion near UCEs predicted up to 34.8% of the variation in the termite net diversification rate. Overall, these results supported TEs as an important contributor to species diversification. More broadly, this study provided a phylogenomic approach to quantify TE activity in the deep past.

title: Temporal Community Assembly of Bacteria and Protists in Different Habitats of a Mountain Lake
content:
ABSTRACT
Whether microbial community assembly is primarily deterministic (selection‐driven) or stochastic (dispersal‐driven) remains a central debate in microbial ecology. We investigated community assembly of bacteria and protists and their driving ecological processes in mountain Lake Tovel using a 5‐year 16S and 18S rRNA metabarcoding dataset. The frequencies of assembly mechanisms and their processes depend on the considered temporal scale. We assessed the influence of temporal scale (years, seasons, temporal distances from 1 to 48 months across all years) and year‐pooling (a common strategy in the assessment of assembly patterns) on the inference of community assembly in the upper euphotic (0–3 m), lower euphotic (3–25 m) and deep hypolimnetic (30–35 m) layers. Focusing on single years, bacteria showed more often different assembly mechanisms (both deterministic and stochastic) across layers and years than protists. Year‐pooling hid the inter‐year differences and preserved the signal of the most frequent single‐year process. A lagged effect of water temperature on bacterial community assembly was found, while an immediate effect on protist assembly. Bacterial and protists' niche width was generally independent of year‐pooling and increased with depth. Our study showed that different temporal scales and depth layers should be considered to gain a comprehensive overview on community assembly.

title: Predation risk alters prey caching behavior and resultant tree establishment patterns
content:
Abstract
The drivers of plant dispersal and distribution are poorly understood. For nut‐bearing trees, interactions between seeds and caching granivores can have a strong influence on population dynamics as unrecovered caches often recruit new trees. Granivore‐seed interactions may be constrained by predators as fear alters caching and foraging behavior. We investigated how predation risk affects caching and foraging behavior in fox squirrels (Sciurus niger) and subsequent recruitment patterns of American turkey oak (Quercus laevis) acorns. We marked and tracked acorns to locate fox squirrel cache and consumption points where we assessed fox squirrel perceived predation risk, measured how caching influenced acorn survival and dispersal, and surveyed juvenile oak distributions. Fox squirrels perceived greater risk at caches than consumption points, suggesting predation risk influences caching decisions and cache distribution. Buried acorns survived at higher rates and only buried acorns germinated, though survival did not vary with dispersal distance. Juvenile oaks and cache locations showed similar hump‐shaped patterns of establishment away from nearest potential source trees. We conclude that predation risk indirectly shapes plant establishment by altering granivore behavior.

title: A computational framework for modeling fluid and solid stressesin porous tissues with application to the trabeculated embryonic heart
content:
by Christine Miller Buffinton, James W. Baish

This study provides a framework for efficient solutions of computational fluid-solid interaction models of porous tissue, with a focus on blood flow through the developing heart wall in the critical chamber and valve formation stages, when trabeculation fills much of the ventricles. This porous, trabeculated tissue is the site of complex mechanotransduction processes, but accurately estimating solid and fluid stresses within such intricate geometries is difficult. We addressed this with three levels of modeling and verification. Images of E12.5 mouse ventricles were first obtained through confocal microscopy and 3D reconstruction. These guided creation of explicit pore-scale finite element simulations with fluid-solid interaction. Idealized and image-derived unit cells were analyzed to determine hydraulic permeability. Next, a multi-pore representation of the ventricular wall was solved with full fluid and solid equations. A continuum model based on Brinkman equations then replaced the explicit pore structure, and sensitivity to permeability was evaluated in terms of fluid flow in the open channel and porous region. Permeabilities obtained from unit cell simulations followed trends from Kozeny-Carman solid-pore and fiber theory for the rigid case, while simulations for hyperelastic unit-cell material quantified the effects of tissue elasticity. Comparison of continuum and explicit model results showed the Brinkman equation, which incorporates the diffusion of shear stress from flow in the free fluid into the porous media, but not explicitly inertial effects, could significantly improve the accuracy of continuum models compared to Darcy's law. A 3D model of blood flow through the ventricles of the developing mouse heart demonstrated the application of the technique to more realistic geometry, showed locations of peak solid and shear stress, and produced physiologically reasonable flow. Furthermore, we developed methodologies to estimate local wall shear and solid stress from continuum-based calculations. This approach can enable efficient, whole-organ parametric analyses of fluid flow, circumventing the need for computationally expensive explicit pore modeling.

title: Visuomotor coordination on the road: Low-dimensional representations reveal adaptive, context-dependent reductions in the dimensionality of natural driving behavior
content:
by John Madrid-Carvajal, Shadi Derakhshan, Peter König

The brain’s ability to transform complex, high-dimensional sensory and motor inputs into coordinated, goal-directed behavior remains a central challenge in neuroscience research. Current research suggests that behavior is generated through patterns within a low-dimensional structure. What visuomotor patterns underlie complex, unconstrained behaviors such as driving, and how stereotypical they are, remain poorly understood. Driving involves complex perception-action interactions, which we hypothesize are specific to the driver’s role and adapt to task demands. Here, we unfold these dynamics using an immersive virtual drive that recreates ten hazardous on-road events. We collected eye, head, and vehicle movements from participants assigned to either a manual or an automated driving condition. From the behavioral movements of 284 drivers, we constructed a common time-resolved behavioral state space based on collective variance, computed via principal component analysis across participants. The obtained low-dimensional representation thus captures generalized visuomotor coordination strategies. We then characterized the evolving low-dimensional structure with cosine similarity and various measures of effective dimensionality. We tested whether leading components contained condition-specific information using discriminant analysis. Throughout the entire drive, few components accounted for most of the variance in behavior, and effective dimensionality decreased reliably around critical events, indicating tighter coordination between perceptual and motor variables. During periods of low effective dimensionality, the contributions of eye, head, steering, and vehicle heading reorganized toward leading dimensions in a task-dependent manner. Across events, between-subject similarity was partially stable and stronger among manual drivers. This reorganization also made behaviors more distinct across driving conditions, enabling better classification of driving modes using only the first two components. These results show that naturalistic driving is supported by shared low-dimensional visuomotor coordination strategies that are flexibly reshaped by contextual demands, and provide a principled behavioral framework for linking neural manifolds, human driver models, and the design of adaptive automated vehicles.

title: High-resolution paleobiome reconstructions highlight ecological and historical dynamics underpinning global terrestrial vertebrate diversity
content:
by Alexander Skeels, Julian Rogger, Marcel Cardillo, Alexander Farnsworth, Daniel J. Lunt, Dirk Nikolaus Karger

Past climate change has repeatedly reshaped Earth’s biomes, yet how their expansion and contraction influence biodiversity patterns through time remains unclear. Competing hypotheses propose that either historical biome area has a strong influence on diversity, or that biodiversity responds rapidly to environmental change, such that present-day biome area and energy are sufficient to explain diversity patterns. Progress in testing these ideas has been limited by sparse and inconsistent proxy data and the coarse resolution of existing paleoclimate models. Here, we reconstructed global biome histories for the Cenozoic (66–0 Ma) by downscaling five different paleoclimate simulations. Estimates of change in biome area through time were generally consistent among alternative climate models and with the empirical proxy record. Accounting for variation among models, we found that present-day area and energy were consistently better predictors of vertebrate diversity than historical measures. These findings suggest biodiversity tracks the ecological limits set by shifting biomes, leaving sparse legacy of past dynamics. Our results highlight the importance of integrating multiple paleoclimate reconstructions when assessing the historical drivers of biodiversity.

title: Dynamism under the hood: Coevolutionary maintenance of variation in hosts and parasites
content:
by Andrea L. Graham, David A. Chang van Oordt

Why do hosts and parasites vary so much? A new study in PLOS Biology reveals that infection outcomes strongly depend upon interacting effects of host and parasite genotypes, offering an evolutionary explanation for profound and persistent variability. Why do hosts and parasites vary so much? This Primer explores a new study in PLOS Biology revealing that infection outcomes strongly depend upon interacting effects of host and parasite genotypes, offering an evolutionary explanation for profound and persistent variability.

title: Mapping the topographic organization of the human zona incerta using diffusion MRI
content: The zona incerta (ZI) is a deep brain region originally described by Auguste Forel as an ‘immensely confusing area about which nothing can be said’. Despite the elusive nature of this structure, mounting evidence supports the role of the ZI and surrounding regions across a diverse range of brain functions and as a candidate target for neuromodulatory therapies. Using in vivo diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and data-driven connectivity, we identify a topographic organization between the ZI and neocortex. Specifically, our methods identify a rostral–caudal gradient predominantly connecting the frontopolar and ventral prefrontal cortices with the rostral ZI, and the primary sensorimotor cortices with the caudal ZI. Moreover, we demonstrate how clustering and gradient approaches build complementary evidence including facilitating the mapping of a central region of the ZI, connected with the dorsal prefrontal cortex. These results were shown to be replicable across multiple datasets and at the individual subject level, building evidence for the important role of the ZI in mediating frontal lobe-associated tasks, ranging from motor to cognitive to emotional control. Finally, we consider the impact of this topographic organization on the refinement of neuromodulatory targets. These results pave the way for an increasingly detailed understanding of ZI substructures, and considerations for in vivo targeting of the ZI for neuromodulation.

title: Large language models poorly capture how word order shapes representations of sentence meaning in the human brain
content: Large language models based on the transformer architecture are now capable of producing human-like language. But do they encode and process linguistic meaning in a human-like way? Here, we address this question by analysing 7T fMRI data from 30 participants reading 108 sentences each. These sentences are carefully designed to disentangle sentence structure from word meaning, thereby testing whether transformer representations of sentence meaning resemble those formed by the brain. Using representational similarity analysis, we compared representations from eight transformers and eleven other semantic models to brain activity in language regions of interest. We found that while transformer models match brain representations better than models that completely ignore word order, all transformers poorly match human brain representations of sentences that require sensitivity to structural relations such as semantic roles (who did what to whom). Further, transformers were significantly inferior to models explicitly designed to encode the structural relations between words. Our results provide insight into the nature of sentence representation in the brain, highlighting the critical role of sentence structure. They also cast doubt on the claim that transformers represent sentence meaning similarly to the human brain.

title: Correction: Targeted degradation of aberrant tau in frontotemporal dementia patient-derived neuronal cell models
Morphology and ultrastructure of pharyngeal sense organs of Drosophila larvae
content: This study provides a comprehensive ultrastructural analysis of the pharyngeal sensory system in Drosophila melanogaster larvae, focusing on the four major pharyngeal sense organs: the ventral pharyngeal sensilla (VPS), dorsal pharyngeal sensilla (DPS), dorsal pharyngeal organ (DPO), and posterior pharyngeal sensilla (PPS). Our analysis revealed 15 sensilla across these organs, comprising four mechanosensory, nine chemosensory, and two dual-function sensilla. We identified 35 Type I neurons (6 mechanosensory and 29 chemosensory) and 6 Type II neurons with putative chemosensory functions. Additional sensory structures, including papilla sensilla and chordotonal organs in the cephalopharyngeal region, were characterized. This detailed mapping and classification of pharyngeal sensory structures completes their structural characterization and provides a foundation for future anatomical and functional studies of sensory perception in insects. This work represents a significant step toward a complete analysis of the larval sensory system, providing new opportunities for investigating how an organism processes sensory information to navigate and interact with its environment.

title: Modulation of human dorsal root ganglion neuron excitability by Nav1.7 inhibition
content: Nav1.7 voltage-gated sodium channels are strongly expressed in human primary pain-sensing neurons (nociceptors), and selective Nav1.7 inhibitors have been developed as possible therapeutic agents for treating pain, so far with disappointing clinical results. In contrast, a selective Nav1.8 channel inhibitor (suzetrigine) has had successful clinical trials. Because nociceptors express both Nav1.7 and Nav1.8 channels, it is of interest to compare effects of Nav1.7 and Nav1.8 inhibitors on the excitability of human nociceptors. To compare with previous results with suzetrigine, we characterized the effects of a selective Nav1.7 inhibitor, AM-2099, on action potential generation and repetitive firing of dissociated human dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, studied at 37°C. Inhibition of Nav1.7 channels by 600 nM AM-2099 generally produced a substantial depolarizing shift of action potential threshold, an increase in rheobase, a decrease in action potential upstroke velocity, decrease in action potential peak, and prolongation of the refractory period. Compared to inhibition of Nav1.8 channels, inhibition of Nav1.7 channels had larger effects on threshold and maximal upstroke velocity, while action potential peak was reduced similarly by both. Nav1.8 inhibition produced much more dramatic reduction of repetitive firing than Nav1.7 inhibition. The results show that although the excitability of human DRG neurons is affected by inhibition of Nav1.7 channels, most notably by an increase in threshold and increase in refractory period, repetitive firing of the neurons in response to strong stimuli is little affected.

title: Climate warming boosts frequency and intensity of southern Africa’s rainfall extremes
content:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02772-0

Extreme southward swings of the South Indian convergence zone (a major source of rainfall across southern Africa) can trigger devastating floods. Climate-model projections indicate that these swings might occur twice as often in the twenty-first century as in the previous century and produce more intense rainfall, owing to an increased land–sea temperature contrast and poleward intensification of atmospheric circulation.
